title: Batching and epochs
goals: Distinguish an example a batch an update and an epoch
Trace parameter changes across successive batches
Calculate update counts and aggregate unequal batch losses correctly

prerequisite.prompt: Week 12 printed states numbered 0 to 4. How many parameter updates occurred?
prerequisite.answer: Four updates occurred. State zero was the initial model before training.

vocabulary: A group of training examples used together to calculate one gradient here
One application of the gradient and learning rate to the current parameters
One pass through all training examples under the stated sampling rule
The intended number of examples in each batch with a possible smaller final batch

blocks.text: In Week 12 every update used both training examples. We now keep the same network h = ReLU(x), y = vh, with only v trained, and divide the data into batches. In this lesson each nonempty batch produces exactly one update. An epoch visits every training example exactly once, without replacement. These rules make the counts unambiguous.

Imagine five fictional records A through E in fixed order. With batch size 2, the groups are [A, B], [C, D] and [E]. Keep the smaller last batch. One epoch has three batches and three updates; two epochs have six updates and ten example visits.

When the last batch is retained, updates per epoch equal the row count divided by batch size rounded up. A program that drops the final incomplete batch follows a different rule and omits examples in that pass. Record the rule instead of silently changing the denominator.

Use the two fictional pairs A = (1, 2) and B = (2, 4), start v = 0 and rate 0.1. For one pair with hidden value h, squared-error gradient is 2 times (vh - target) times h. For a batch, average these gradients at the same current v. Apply one update, then recompute for the next batch.

blocks.title: Optional Python check
blocks.text:
def epoch(v, rows, size, rate):
    if not rows or size < 1:
        raise ValueError("Need rows and positive batch size")
    trace = []
    for start in range(0, len(rows), size):
        batch = rows[start:start + size]
        hs = [max(0.0, x) for x, target in batch]
        gradient = sum(2 * (v * h - target) * h
                       for h, (x, target) in zip(hs, batch)) / len(batch)
        v = v - rate * gradient
        trace.append(v)
    return trace

rows = [(1.0, 2.0), (2.0, 4.0)]
print([round(v, 6) for v in epoch(0.0, rows, 1, 0.1)])  # [0.4, 1.68]
print([round(v, 6) for v in epoch(0.0, rows, 2, 0.1)])  # [1.0]

Assume finite numeric pairs, integer size and finite rate. With size 1, A gives gradient -4 and new v = 0.4. B then uses 0.4, giving prediction 0.8, residual -3.2 and gradient -12.8, so v becomes 1.68. With size 2, both gradients are evaluated at v = 0; their mean is -10, producing v = 1.

blocks.title: One pass can contain different numbers of updates
blocks.caption: All three passes visit two examples. The reversed order happens to end at the same value for these proportional targets; that coincidence is not a general order-invariance rule.

blocks.label: For B then A separately, show both gradients and new parameter values. Why does one epoch still contain two updates?

lesson.title: Compare losses at a shared snapshot

blocks.text: Batch losses observed during training can refer to different parameter values and different examples. They are not automatically the full training loss of the final model. To compare final models, freeze each one and evaluate every training example again. Here full training MSE is 2.5 times (v - 2) squared: at v = 1 it is 2.5, and at v = 1.68 it is 0.256. These are training results only.

Even at one fixed model, averaging batch means without their sizes gives the wrong dataset mean when batches have different lengths. Suppose the squared errors on A to E are [1, 1, 4, 4, 9]. Batch means for lengths 2, 2, 1 are [1, 4, 9]. Full MSE is (2 times 1 + 2 times 4 + 1 times 9) / 5 = 3.8, not (1 + 4 + 9) / 3. Use example counts as weights.

Equal epochs mean equal example visits under our rule, but changing batch size changes the number of updates. A comparison should report both counts, starting values, order, learning rate and the rule for the last batch. Neither smaller batches nor more updates guarantee better independent performance.

blocks.label: Two teams train on five rows for two epochs. One uses size 2 and the other size 5, retaining every row. Are their example visits and update counts equal? Explain what to record.

blocks.text: Next week holds the batch rule fixed while comparing learning rates.

workbook.title: Count a partial batch
workbook.prompt: For 10 rows, batch size 4 and three epochs, retaining the final batch, list batch lengths and count total updates and example visits.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Batch lengths 4, 4, 2; three updates per epoch, nine total updates and 30 example visits.

workbook.title: Repair a stale gradient
workbook.prompt: For A then B separately in the lesson, a learner computes both gradients at v = 0, then applies them to get v = 2. Explain the error and give the correct final value.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The second gradient must use v = 0.4. Using -16 from the old state is stale; the current B gradient is -12.8 and the final v is 1.68.

workbook.title: Combine unequal batches
workbook.prompt: At one frozen model, batches of sizes 3 and 1 have mean squared errors 2 and 10. Find the full MSE and explain why the average of 2 and 10 is wrong.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Full MSE is (3 times 2 + 10) / 4 = 4. The unweighted average 6 gives the single-row batch too much weight.

workbook.title: Test order on a new case independently
workbook.prompt: Use A = (1, 1), B = (2, 0), h = ReLU(x), y = vh, v = 0 and rate 0.1. Train with size 1 for one epoch in A then B order, then restart at 0 and reverse the order. Show gradients and parameter values. Compare the final values.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: A then B: A gradient -2 gives v = 0.2; B residual 0.4 gives gradient 1.6 and v = 0.04. B then A: B gradient 0 keeps v = 0; A gradient -2 gives v = 0.2. Both see the same rows but finish differently.

workbook.title: Audit an epoch claim
workbook.prompt: A program processes 11 rows using size 4 and drops the last incomplete batch. How many examples did it visit and how many updates occurred? What must its report disclose?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: It visits eight rows in two batches and performs two updates. Three rows are omitted; it did not complete a full pass under this lesson definition. Report the drop rule and actual visits.

teacher.background: Use two 45-minute sessions to separate counting from numerical training. Keep the frozen hidden layer from Week 12. Have students move paper record cards into batches before doing arithmetic. The coincident final values for the proportional-target example require the independent counterexample; do not teach that ordering is generally irrelevant.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Retrieve states versus updates, then arrange five cards into batches of two.
Count batches, updates and visits for the table and W1; discuss retaining the final group.
Trace A then B at current v. Complete W2 and identify exactly where the stale gradient arose.
Run or trace the code and compare the full-batch update with the two singleton updates.
Complete the guided reverse-order trace and mark its coincidental equal endpoint.
Calculate fixed-model loss and use W3 to weight unequal batch means.
Collect W4 independently, requiring a fresh reset for the reverse-order run.
Discuss W5 and the exit response, then assess the fresh retry after targeted feedback.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided: B at v = 0 gives gradient -16 and v = 1.6. A then gives residual -0.4, gradient -0.8 and v = 1.68. Two batches each cause one update. Exit: both teams visit ten examples. Size 2 produces six updates; size 5 produces two. Record both budgets and all training settings.
misconceptions: One epoch always means one update
Only a full-data batch gives one update per epoch in this procedure.
Reuse all gradients from the start of an epoch
Recompute at the parameter value before each batch update.
At one fixed model, weight each batch mean by the number of examples in that batch.
teacher.assessment: W4 requires the two traces and final values 0.04 and 0.2. Fresh retry: A = (1, 2), B = (1, 0), start v = 0, rate 0.25, singleton batches. A then B gives gradients -4 and 2, values 1 and 0.5. Reverse order gives gradients 0 and -4, values 0 and 1. Ask students to name the reset and explain the order effect.
teacher.support: Provide separate boxes for old v, batch gradient and new v; allow calculators. Extension: at a fixed v, prove that the row-count-weighted mean of batch gradients equals the full-data mean gradient. Explain why successive updates with changed v are a different procedure.
